title: Chapter VI

teacherSummary.text: Charlotte argues Jane should show more affection to secure Bingley, since 'happiness in marriage is entirely a matter of chance.' Darcy begins to admire Elizabeth's 'fine eyes,' and Miss Bingley teases him about it.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter VI,” how does Austen show strategy in courtship? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter VI develops the idea of strategy in courtship. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and foreshadowing shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses characterization in Chapter VI to complicate the reader's understanding of strategy in courtship. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter VI within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of strategy in courtship responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter VI as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of strategy in courtship. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

segments.activity: Quick-write and share on the opening question.
segments.script: Good morning, readers. Before we open the book, take three minutes and write your honest answer to this: Do you agree with Charlotte that happiness in marriage is a matter of chance? There is no wrong answer yet; we will test our ideas against the text today.

segments.activity: Model pronouncing, defining and using five key words in context.
segments.script: Today's words include complaisance, performs, conceals, porridge, simpleton. Watch how I figure out a word from its sentence before I check the dictionary. Here is the line: ““He is indeed—but considering the inducement, my dear Miss Eliza, we cannot wonder at his complaisance; for who would object to such a partner?”” My guess comes from the clues around it; the dictionary says: Disposition to please or oblige.

segments.activity: Present background, then the significance of the chapter.
segments.script: Let me give you some background that the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Women could not propose; they had to signal interest within strict propriety. Now, why does this chapter matter? Charlotte's pragmatic view of marriage foreshadows her own choice later; Darcy's interest is the novel's first reversal. As you listen, jot one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Foreshadowing, Irony.
segments.script: Let's read this passage together. I will read the first sentence; you track along. Every time you spot characterization, mark it. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice here? I will collect three ideas on the board and we will choose the strongest one together, using the evidence.
